General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dualshockers ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 10 Video Game Rivals I Was Never Actually Mad At

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that truth be told, I have a bit of a thing for villains who aren't entirely wrong.
  • I will say that most of these are still very much ultimately in the wrong.
  • Note: There are spoilers for every game on this list, including some very major ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that truth be told, I have a bit of a thing for villains who aren't entirely wrong. Give me an antagonist with a tragic backstory and a motive I can halfway get behind, and I will spend the entire final boss fight feeling a little bit bad about winning it. Some of the games on this list are old, which shows you how profoundly they impacted me at the time I played them.

I will say that most of these are still very much ultimately in the wrong. It’s usually their methods I have issues with, ranging from questionable to horrific. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Nonetheless, I can’t bring myself to be angry at them, because they are somewhat justified in their actions, so let's take a look at ten video game rivals I was never actually mad at.

Note: There are spoilers for every game on this list, including some very major ones.

In a recent development, N's whole philosophy is quite uncomfortable when you really think about it: he wants every Pokémon set free, because he believes they are suffering in the care of their trainers. And I'm not being funny, but he kind of has a point. We have spent 30 years catching animals, keeping them in tiny balls and making them fight each other for badges. The entire anime’s premise is that Pikachu didn’t like being stuck in a Poké Ball!

It has been revealed that N is so very intriguing, right from the first encounter. Black and White had already given you two rivals in Cheren and Bianca before you even leave your hometown, and yet here is a third one, with his own battle theme and a design that looks nothing like anyone else's in a Pokémon game. He can also hear what Pokémon are saying, and when he tells you that yours genuinely like you, you believe him.

Sources indicate that he reveals himself as the king of Team Plasma on the Ferris wheel in Nimbasa City, and later on, a legendary dragon chooses him without him ever throwing a single Poké Ball. You still beat him, though.

Recent findings suggest that it then turns out that Ghetsis found him abandoned in the woods as a child, raised him alongside Pokémon that had been hurt by humans and turned him into a puppet king, all so Ghetsis could be the only person in Unova with Pokémon. The poor boy never stood a chance. As someone who will never play a Pokémon game without her starter, I'd like to think I'm one of the good ones, but I do understand his concerns.

Kirby: Nightmare in Dream Land is the rare case where the hero causes all the trouble. King Dedede steals the Star Rod from the Fountain of Dreams, breaks it into seven pieces and hands them out to his friends, and suddenly, nobody in Dream Land can dream anymore. Considering this is the same king who once stole all of Dream Land's food, Kirby assumes the worst, and quite frankly, I can't blame him.

In a recent development, the problem is that Kirby doesn't even let him explain. When the two of them meet at the fountain, Kirby refuses to listen to a single word and marches off to collect every piece. As far as we know, Dedede simply stays at the fountain the entire time, keeping an eye on things.

Then Kirby comes back, beats him and puts the Star Rod back in place, whilst Dedede hangs on to his feet and begs him not to. Out comes Nightmare, who Dedede had been keeping sealed away the whole time. Instead of saying "I told you so", he inhales Kirby and spits him into the sky to go and fix it, which is a lot more grace than I would have managed.

In a recent development, lilith's backstory is a lot more relatable than you'd expect from the daughter of Mephisto. She was created as little more than an extension of her father, grew tired of the Eternal Conflict between Heaven and Hell, and ran off with the angel Inarius to create Sanctuary: a hidden world where renegade angels and demons could live in peace. They had a son, the others had children too, and those children became the Nephalem.

Industry observers note that now, the Nephalem turned out to be far more powerful than their parents, and that made the renegades nervous. Some of them argued that the children would draw the attention of Heaven and Hell and should be destroyed, and Lilith did not take that well: she hunted the renegades down and slaughtered angels and demons alike. A number of Nephalem died along the way, too, and I can’t lie: she kind of loses me here a little.

According to recent reports, subsequently, Inarius couldn't bring himself to kill her, so he banished her to the Void and used the Worldstone to weaken the Nephalem, which meant they eventually developed into what became mankind. I will note that her plans for her children weren't exactly selfless, either, since she always saw them as her own army. Still, the man she created them with was ready to wipe them out, and I can see how that might put someone in a bad mood for a few thousand years.

Industry observers note that maruki is the kind of man I'd trust with my problems instantly, which is exactly what makes him so difficult to fight. He joins Shujin Academy as the fresh school counsellor after the Kamoshida scandal, he is incredibly easy to talk to, and he genuinely wants to help. He's also a researcher in cognitive psience, which is never a good sign in Persona 5.

His story starts long before he meets the Phantom Thieves. When his girlfriend Rumi fell into a catatonic state after her parents were killed in a break-in, Maruki awakened a Persona that could rewrite cognition and used it to save her. It worked, but she forgot the trauma and him along with it, and he stepped out of her life so he wouldn't bring any of it back.

In a recent development, from there, his dream grew into a world without grief or suffering, where everyone gets the life they always wanted. The catch is that nobody gets asked: he convinced Sumire that she was her late sister Kasumi, and he'd happily do the same to everyone else. That takes away free will and the chance to grow through hardship, and he crossed that line long before we ever got involved. He isn't after money or power, though, and he truly believes he's helping, which is why his Palace was the one I least wanted to break into.

According to recent reports, sure, Sin is evil and the substantial bad, and thus the villain, but technically, we’re talking about every summoner who ever set out to destroy it. For hundreds of years, summoners travelled across Spira with a guardian or two, learned to call the aeons at every temple along the way and eventually made their way to Zanarkand for the Final Summoning. Once there, they would sacrifice a guardian to finally defeat Sin.

The problem is what happens afterwards. That guardian becomes the Final Aeon, and once Sin is destroyed, Yu Yevon possesses it and turns it into the next Sin. The Calm that everyone celebrates is really just the new Sin being created and slowly gaining its power, and so the whole cycle starts over again.

So why did they keep doing this for hundreds of years? Well, nobody knew until it was far too late. The sacrifice of the summoner and a guardian was common knowledge, but the fact that the guardian would become one with Sin was not, and summoners only learned the truth once they met Yunalesca in Zanarkand. By that point, you've gathered your aeons, travelled across the entire world and are about to go toe-to-toe with the biggest bad there is. I can't really blame a single one of them for going through with it.

It has been revealed that fou-Lu does not make a great first impression. Within minutes of waking up, he has two soldiers killed for bragging that the Fou Empire could crush dragons, and he looks rather pleased with himself about it. To be fair to him, he has just woken up from a centuries-long nap, and nobody is at their best first thing in the morning.

He is the God Emperor, the other half of Ryu and the founder of the Fou Empire, who went to sleep with a promise that he would take back the throne once he awoke. The current Emperor would rather he didn't. General Yohm hunts him across the country, sets forests on fire and throws monster after monster at him until Fou-Lu crashes into the woods, barely alive.

In a recent development, he wakes up in a little farming village, where a kind woman named Mami takes care of him, and for a while, it's genuinely sweet. Then imperial troops show up, Mami helps him escape, and the Empire fires at him. Before he blacks out, he realises that Mami's life was used to power the weapon. Wanting to wipe out humanity might still be a bit much, but quite frankly, I'd be grumpy too.

Loewe's backstory is incredibly bleak: he grew up in Hamel, a small Erebonian village near the Liberl border, and he was in love with Joshua's older sister, Karin. When the village was massacred to start a war, he lost his family and Karin, and he was right there when it happened. That alone would be enough to send anyone down a dark path.

What really gets me, though, is what happened afterwards: once the war was over, the massacre was quietly covered up, and the official story was that a landslide had destroyed the road to the village. Loewe had no way of seeking justice and nobody to even acknowledge what happened, so he and Joshua made Karin's grave themselves.

So he joined Ouroboros, became its Enforcer No. II, the Sword Emperor, and set out to make the world face the injustices it would rather sweep under the rug. He is cold and terrifyingly strong whenever he highlights up, but he still looks out for Joshua for Karin's sake. Without spoiling too much, finding out who was really behind Hamel only makes it worse.

I have played Tales of Symphonia more times than I can count, and Mithos gets more tragic with every single playthrough. Long before the game begins, he and his sister Martel were half-elves, hated by humans and elves alike, and driven out of their home because of it. Even so, they went on to end the Ancient Kharlan War together with Kratos and Yuan, and became heroes.

Then Martel was killed, and her dying wish for a world without discrimination turned into something rather sinister in his hands: the Age of Lifeless Beings, where everyone would be the same emotionless being, so that there would be nothing left to discriminate against. Over 4,000 years, that idea only gets worse. By the end, he is mostly fixated on bringing his sister back.

According to recent reports, the game clearly wants you to see him as the villain, but it also makes you understand him, and that is what makes him so well written. Raine and Genis have to hide that they're half-elves to protect her teaching job and his education, and even they can't fully dismiss his points. Tales of Symphonia is quite heavy-handed about discrimination, I will say, but it was pretty profound.

Recent findings suggest that psaro's motivation is almost sweet, as far as wanting to wipe out humanity goes: he is in love with Rose, an elf who cries ruby tears. Naturally, greedy humans want those tears, not knowing that they break very easily, so Psaro builds her a little tower far away from all of them. Rose, meanwhile, keeps asking him to make peace with humans, which he refuses to do.

Sources indicate that he isn't innocent, mind you. Egged on by his advisor Aamon, and after hearing that a human hero is prophesied to defeat him, he starts hunting down young humans, which is how the Hero's village gets destroyed at the start of Chapter 5. When Rose is then killed by humans, he loses it completely and transforms himself into Psaro the Manslayer.

Recent findings suggest that the remakes added a sixth chapter, and that is why he made this list. You find a World Tree flower that can bring someone back from the dead, use it on Rose, and her tears turn Psaro back to normal. It also turns out that Aamon arranged her death to take over monsterkind himself, so Psaro joins your party to deal with him. He even got his own game in 2023, Dragon Quest Monsters: The Dark Prince, which feels like a well-earned redemption arc.

Saturos and Menardi were right, and boy, does that annoy me. For the entire first Golden Sun, they are the villains: they raid Mt. Aleph, steal the Elemental Stars and set off to light the four Elemental Lighthouses, which would release Alchemy back into the world. Alchemy was sealed away because it could destroy everything in the wrong hands, so naturally, you chase them across the continent and stop them.

Recent findings suggest that then The Lost Age hands you Felix, who has been travelling with them all along, and the whole story flips. Without Alchemy, the world of Weyard is slowly dying, and its edges are crumbling into the void. Their hometown of Prox sits right next to the Mars Lighthouse at the far north of the world, and it is drifting closer to that edge by the day. Menardi's younger sister Karst and her partner Agatio carry on where the first two left off, because their entire village depends on it.

Instead of explaining any of that, they went for sneaky and threatening, and they even kept Felix's family locked up in Prox to make sure he'd cooperate. I do understand why, though: nobody was going to believe two strangers claiming that the world was falling apart, especially when hardly anyone could ever travel far enough to see it. A little more communication would have saved everyone a lot of trouble.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One unofficial GTA 6 PC port has been scrapped, hours after major progress in getting the game up and running was shown, as its lead quits and alleges that Rockstar Games has taken down the project's Discord server.
  • Industry observers note that project Leonida was one of the main GTA 6 recompilation efforts, and yesterday, as notorious leaker Cyberleek dropped an executable file for the Xbox build of the game they'd shared last week, it seemed like it wouldn't be long before the fan-made PC port was functional.
  • In the hours that followed, it'd seem even more progress was made.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One unofficial GTA 6 PC port has been scrapped, hours after major progress in getting the game up and running was shown, as its lead quits and alleges that Rockstar Games has taken down the project's Discord server.

Industry observers note that project Leonida was one of the main GTA 6 recompilation efforts, and yesterday, as notorious leaker Cyberleek dropped an executable file for the Xbox build of the game they'd shared last week, it seemed like it wouldn't be long before the fan-made PC port was functional. The devs behind Leonida never expected things to work immediately, but mere hours after the EXE file was dropped, an update in the Discord server claimed: "The game almost boots. Black screen, audio cuts off.".

In the hours that followed, it'd seem even more progress was made. One video shared on Reddit, apparently posted on the Leonida Discord server, appears to show the full opening sequence and the first-time game setup running on PC. However, don't expect any further updates from the project – or at least, not from its original creator – as the Discord server has now completely disappeared, and the project's lead states they're "stepping away" from it entirely.

"I quit guys. I'm sorry," NotRexed writes on Twitter. "I really want to make cool stuff but every single time shit happens that I can't control so I'm stepping away. Thank you everybody, especially in the discord that allowed me to have this opportunity.".

Recent findings suggest that in a follow-up post, they claim that Rockstar was behind the Discord server's takedown, saying: "Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I've mentioned before, I'm a 15-year-old kid. Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle-aged men yell and complain to you on Discord. Goodbye." Their original GitHub repository has also vanished, though others' clones of Leonida still appear to be live.

In a recent development, even with the original version of Leonida scrapped, though, there are still other projects racing to be the first to actually work. In fact, there's a whole tracker dedicated to monitoring the progress of various projects and how close they are to being ready to work. One such project recently noted: "The title boots, runs its menus at its own 30 fps and loads the world, where rendering fails.".

While none are working yet, I still expect takedowns aplenty in the coming days and weeks, even if it's exceedingly difficult to completely wipe something from the internet once it's been posted.

In a recent development, even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Recent findings suggest that today, publisher Koei Tecmo has confirmed that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

Sources indicate that on Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

According to recent reports, nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”.

If you’re curious about the challenging and very rewarding action RPG, start with these gameplay tips, and don’t be shy to call upon a friend (or stranger) for help using our co-op guide.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, america's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up.
  • In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission.
  • America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, america's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up. More electric vehicles, increased electricity use in heavy industry, and the explosive growth of data centers are driving demand higher, putting additional pressure on an infrastructure system that is already falling behind.

In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission. The problem could have major consequences for electricity prices, grid reliability, and the nation's economic future.

America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.

According to recent reports, A major concern is the extremely slow pace of transmission construction. Over the past five years, the continental United States has added an average of only about 500 miles of high-voltage transmission lines annually. Research suggests the country needs approximately 5,000 miles each year to triple the size of its interregional transmission network by 2050 and accommodate future electricity demand.

Industry observers note that that means the U.S. is building latest high-voltage transmission lines at just one-tenth of the estimated pace needed.

In a recent development, high-voltage transmission lines serve as the highways of the electricity system, carrying large amounts of power over long distances from generating facilities to communities and businesses. Connecting regional grids allows electricity to flow more easily between areas, helping balance supply and demand when local power production falls short.

It has been revealed that studies have shown that larger, better-connected electricity networks can reduce costs for consumers while also lowering the risk of catastrophic blackouts. When one region experiences a power shortage, electricity from another region can help keep the lights on.

Despite these advantages, expanding the nation's transmission infrastructure has proved extraordinarily difficult.

The Biggest Obstacle Isn't Technology.

According to the researchers (Madeline Yozwiak, David G. Victor, and M. Granger Morgan), the main barriers to modernizing America's power grid are political and regulatory rather than technological.

Responsibility for approving major transmission projects is divided among federal agencies, state governments, local authorities, and private companies. Each has its own priorities and interests, creating numerous opportunities for proposed power lines to be delayed or blocked.

In a recent development, existing electric utilities can also have financial reasons to resist stronger connections between regions. Greater competition from electricity suppliers elsewhere could weaken their influence over local markets, reducing the incentive to support projects that would benefit the broader electricity system.

As a result, even transmission projects that could lower costs and improve reliability across the country can struggle to gain approval.

Three Ways to Fix America's Power Grid Crisis.

To address the growing shortfall, the researchers recommend a three-part strategy combining stronger government action, modern transmission technologies, international cooperation, and regulatory reform.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Make better use of existing federal powers and advanced technologies.

According to recent reports, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Department of Energy (DOE) already have legal authorities that could help move important transmission projects forward. The researchers argue that these agencies should use those powers more effectively, including identifying transmission corridors of national importance and addressing disputes that prevent projects from receiving state-level approval.

It has been revealed that technological improvements could also dramatically increase the amount of electricity the grid can carry. One approach, known as reconductoring, involves replacing existing power line conductors with more advanced materials capable of transmitting more electricity without necessarily requiring entirely new routes.

Recent findings suggest that other advances, including newer High-Voltage Direct Current (VSC-HVDC) systems, offer additional ways to move large amounts of electricity efficiently. The researchers suggest that modern transmission technologies could double or even triple capacity.

According to recent reports, underground high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables offer another promising option. These systems can carry substantial amounts of electricity over long distances and could potentially be installed along existing highways and railroad corridors. Using these established routes could help avoid some of the land-use disputes and approval challenges that often delay conventional transmission projects.

2. Learn from countries that have already overcome similar obstacles.

The United States trails several international counterparts in building long-distance HVDC infrastructure and coordinating electricity transmission across regional and national boundaries.

Other countries have demonstrated that large transmission projects can move forward despite complicated political approval processes. Some have also successfully deployed underground HVDC systems on a large scale.

Rather than developing every solution independently, the researchers suggest that the U.S. should study these international experiences and adapt approaches that have already proved successful.

It has been revealed that one proposal is to establish an international forum involving electricity regulators and other experts, potentially led by organizations such as the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC). Such a forum could help American policymakers identify effective regulatory practices, planning strategies, and technologies used elsewhere.

3. Create a national commission to break the political deadlock.

The researchers also recommend establishing a Presidential-Congressional Transmission Commission to address the political and regulatory conflicts that have slowed grid expansion for decades.

Modeled on previous successful bipartisan commissions, the proposed group would bring together key stakeholders to negotiate difficult decisions and develop a coordinated proposal for reform.

Its responsibilities would include recommending changes to state and federal laws, examining whether FERC should receive broader authority over the locations of new transmission projects, and developing financial incentives for companies that lead new construction.

The commission could also recommend financial rewards for communities that host transmission infrastructure, helping ensure that local residents share in the benefits of projects that serve larger regions.

Why America's Power Grid Crisis Could Get Worse.

The researchers emphasize that the underlying challenge is not a lack of engineering solutions. Instead, the country's divided decision-making system allows individual stakeholders to obstruct projects that could deliver substantial nationwide benefits.

"The fundamental challenge isn't technical, it's jurisdictional. Authority is divided among federal, state, and private entities, each with distinct priorities. When every stakeholder possesses the power to say no, even high-value projects that benefit the entire nation struggle to move forward," the authors warn.

Their assessment suggests that simply continuing with the existing system of overlapping regulations and fragmented authority will not be enough to meet America's growing electricity needs.

Without meaningful changes to how transmission projects are planned, approved, and built, the United States risks a prolonged infrastructure shortfall. The researchers warn that failing to resolve these problems could weaken electricity reliability and inflict lasting damage on the national economy, even as demand for power continues to climb.

  • The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.
  • Recent findings suggest that the quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of fresh content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one patch on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

Recent findings suggest that in the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of concerns should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

According to recent reports, the first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

Sources indicate that the infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo concerns, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Recent findings suggest that another key area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

Industry observers note that the good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next patch will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported complications.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

For a non-partner side, a later run to Masters would be worth a fixed US$200,000 and a place at Champions US$400,000, Dot Esports reported. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xbox have confirmed that Wolfenstein 3 is indeed in production at Indiana Jones and the Great Circle devs MachineGames and that Doom makers id Software have started work on their next game after losing a bunch of staff to the mass layoffs across Microsoft's gaming division this year.

"A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations," isn't part of the marketing spiel for either of those games. Instead, it's something Xbox CEO Asha Shama has bellowed amid a rant outlining how she sees the company's future.

According to recent reports, the Wolfenstein and id confirmations came as Xbox had a bit of a social media party to commemorate their 25th birthday. Sharma, ever keen to be seen right next to any positive news coming out of the company, confirmed Wolfenstein 3 is in production by posting a photo showing a few lines from its script. Around the same time, she shouted out Doom: The Dark Ages Revelations' incoming Slaughter Mode, adding that "the team is already working on its next game".

The official id Software account responded to note that this next game is being made by their "teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin", and that "it'll be some time before [they're] ready to share more".

We're incredibly excited about our next project, a new game from our teams in Texas and Frankfurt, with game direction once again by Hugo Martin. It'll be some time before we're ready to share more but we can't wait for you to see what we're working on.

Alongside hollering about these couple of games, Sharma put out a 25th anniversary statement which for the most part does the sort of bigging up of Xbox's past you'd expect. Good times were had, we blazed a trail and made lots of money, etcetera. The final section saw the exec attempt to look forward to the next 25 years for Xbox.

"While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically," she wrote. "As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this.

Sources indicate that "Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today's games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982.".

According to recent reports, that certainly sounds a lot like the sales pitch the biggest proponents of generative AI keep wheeling out, while avoiding saying generative AI out loud in the hopes of making it more palatable to folks who might not make the connection. I'm waiting for Sharma to put out another post revealing that she accidentally mixed another section of the Wolfenstein script into her celebratory musings, but I'm not holding my breath.

Xbox parent tech giant Microsoft are still right now subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

#110029. TinyBuild CEO Downplays Threats of AI Game-Cloning

TinyBuild CEO Downplays Threats of AI Game-Cloning

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as part of the ever-growing ingress of AI slop into the gaming industry, a latest threat has recently arisen in the form of AI game-cloning.
  • According to recent reports, developers are taking this threat very seriously.
  • There’s even been rumors that the PC release of Grand Theft Auto 6 could be expedited just to get ahead of the proverbial slop factory that’s already churning out identical open-world crime sandbox games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as part of the ever-growing ingress of AI slop into the gaming industry, a latest threat has recently arisen in the form of AI game-cloning. In a nutshell, a user feeds footage and descriptions of a game into their toaster of choice, as well as more specific data like coding cribbed from released demos, and instructs it to make effectively the same game. The infamous recent example of this was Needle in a Haystack Simulator, a small indie game that, following its announcement, received a deluge of AI-made knock-offs that flooded the Steam store.

According to recent reports, developers are taking this threat very seriously. During the most recent Steam Next Fest, which was already plagued by AI slop, several indie devs decided against releasing demos out of concern that bad actors would churn out knock-offs before they could release their actual games. Some developers have admitted to receiving anonymous extortion threats, saying that if a ransom isn’t paid, the crooks will release an AI knock-off of their game before they can release the real one.

There’s even been rumors that the PC release of Grand Theft Auto 6 could be expedited just to get ahead of the proverbial slop factory that’s already churning out identical open-world crime sandbox games.

Obviously, this is a big problem, and it’s only going to get worse as AI gets smarter, but at least according to game publisher tinyBuild’s CEO Alex Nichiporchik, developers should not be afraid of these malicious duplicates. As he explained in an interview with Gamesindustry.biz, AI may be able to imitate a game’s basic aesthetics, but game feel is another matter.

In a recent development, as Nichiporchik points out, while AI-made knock-offs of existing or confirmed games may have some superficial similarities, such as setting, basic game concepts, or story beats, those elements are only part of what makes a particular game a unique experience. In fact, it’s the “experience” itself that serves as the primary differentiator, and despite its best efforts, AI can’t do much in that department.

Industry observers note that “There's a reason that every kind of AI slop game feels the same," he explained. "It's because when you try to make something from zero, AI will multiply your skills, and zero times a thousand is still zero.”.

There's a reason that every kind of AI slop game feels the same.

Nichiporchik went on to say that, rather than being afraid of having their ideas stolen, developers should consider what they can do to make their games more difficult to duplicate, primarily in how the game handles and in its core gameplay loop.

Industry observers note that as Nichiporchik himself puts it, you could have an entire army of designers and researchers trying to completely duplicate something popular, but it just won’t have that same distinctive zing as the real thing, authentically brought to life by its original creators. It’s not unlike the number of bodies games like Fortnite or Grand Theft Auto have left in their wake as other studios try unsuccessfully to ape their formulas.

“As long as you have great game feel and a great game loop, I think you're going to be OK,” Nichiporchik assured.

Despite his assurances, Nichiporchik admitted that these AI-made games, not unlike fast food, are ubiquitous and rather obnoxious. Part of the problem is that AI knock-offs are basically trying to capitalize on the hype generated by a game’s announcement, as well as promotion like trailers or demos, stealing attention away from the genuine article or even fooling players not in the know into buying the wrong product.

Nichiporchik’s suggestion for this is to narrow the gap between announcement and release. While the standard strategy is to give the hype thrusters time to warm up and let the game accumulate wishlists and word-of-mouth, playing things close to the vest with a faster turnaround seems to work just as well.

Recent findings suggest that as Nichiporchik explained, the most recent game published by tinyBuild, Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, was announcement-ready as early as May, but tinyBuild and Questing Goose Studio decided to wait until August to announce, then release in October instead. That game’s done gangbusters despite somewhat repetitive gameplay, so it seems like the strategy worked out, and without giving bad actors nearly as much time to try to copy their notes.

#110028. A simple metal is hiding a strange latest form of magnetism

A simple metal is hiding a strange latest form of magnetism

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open new possibilities for quantum technology.
  • The material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented.
  • The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open new possibilities for quantum technology. Researchers have found compelling evidence of a rare magnetic state in which electrons behave in unexpected ways, even though the material produces no overall magnetization.

The material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented. This behavior is associated with a phenomenon called p-wave magnetism, an emerging area of research that could eventually help scientists develop latest approaches to controlling electronic properties.

The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound. Unlike many materials previously considered for studying this exotic form of magnetism, it offers researchers a practical way to investigate the underlying physics in detail.

An Unexpected Discovery in a Simple Metal.

The research began about three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden, Germany. Dr. Erjian Cheng successfully grew high-quality single crystals of EuSi, providing the material needed for detailed experiments.

When researchers first examined the crystals using photoemission techniques, which probe the energies and behavior of electrons inside materials, they noticed something unexpected. The magnetic arrangement of the atoms had a remarkably strong influence on the electronic band structure, which describes the energy levels electrons can occupy and helps determine how a material conducts electricity.

It has been revealed that that observation raised an intriguing possibility. Could this simple compound contain an unconventional form of magnetism in which the spin of an electron is connected to the direction it travels?

"When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons," explains Cheng. "That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.".

Answering that question required an international collaboration involving 38 scientists from 19 institutions. Participants included researchers from ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

A Strange Form of Magnetism That Cancels Itself Out.

Ordinary magnets, such as those attached to refrigerators, typically rely on a magnetic arrangement called ferromagnetism. In these materials, many electron spins align in the same direction, producing an overall magnetic field.

At temperatures between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, the magnetic moments of its europium atoms organize themselves into a repeating spiral pattern. These temperatures correspond to roughly minus 400 to minus 348 degrees Fahrenheit.

It has been revealed that each europium atom has a substantial magnetic moment, but their orientations balance one another across the spiral. As a result, the material has no net magnetization in this magnetic phase.

According to recent reports, however, the absence of overall magnetization does not mean magnetism has stopped influencing the electrons. In fact, the researchers found that the spiral arrangement produces a highly unusual electronic structure.

It has been revealed that in the proposed p-wave magnetic state, electrons traveling in opposite directions have opposite spin polarizations. Electron spin is a quantum property that gives electrons magnetic characteristics, although it should not be understood as an electron literally spinning like a tiny ball.

The relationship between an electron's direction of motion and its spin is called an odd-parity spin texture. This means that reversing the electron's momentum also reverses the associated spin polarization.

Other materials can display spin-dependent energy differences because of a phenomenon known as spin-orbit coupling, which connects an electron's motion to its spin. In EuSi, however, the unusual spin structure appears to arise mainly from interactions between magnetic moments and the specific symmetry of their spiral arrangement.

Experiments Reveal Evidence of Rare P-Wave Magnetism.

To determine whether EuSi truly exhibits the predicted magnetic state, the scientists combined several sophisticated experimental methods with theoretical calculations.

First, they used neutron diffraction, a technique that reveals how atoms and magnetic moments are arranged inside a material. These measurements confirmed that the europium magnetic moments form a spiral structure with the symmetry required for p-wave magnetism.

Next, the researchers examined the material using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. This method measures the energies and momenta of electrons, allowing scientists to map the electronic structure.

The results demonstrated that magnetic ordering substantially reorganizes the electron energy levels. In particular, the team observed magnetically driven energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts, indicating an unusually strong influence of magnetism on electron behavior.

The most decisive evidence came from spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which allowed the researchers to examine electron spin polarization directly.

It has been revealed that they observed that the sign of the spin polarization changed across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. These zones are regions of momentum space used by physicists to describe how electrons behave within a repeating magnetic structure.

The team also found that spin polarization became much weaker near locations where theoretical calculations predicted the p-wave spin texture should disappear.

Taken together, the measurements provide compelling experimental evidence consistent with the predicted p-wave magnetic state in EuSi.

A Hidden Magnetic Spiral With Two Different Orientations.

The researchers uncovered another unusual feature of EuSi involving chirality, a scientific term describing handedness.

A familiar example is the difference between a left hand and a right hand. They are mirror images, but they cannot be perfectly superimposed.

Something similar happens with the magnetic spiral inside EuSi. Although the underlying crystal has a centrosymmetric structure, meaning its atomic arrangement is unchanged by inversion through a central point, the magnetic spiral can twist in either of two opposite directions.

These different spiral orientations create magnetic regions, or domains, with opposite handedness.

In a recent development, using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the scientists identified domains measuring approximately ten micrometers across. For perspective, ten micrometers is about one-tenth the thickness of a typical human hair.

When the researchers examined these regions using circularly polarized light, they detected different electronic responses depending on the handedness of the magnetic spiral.

This finding demonstrates that the direction in which the magnetic structure twists is linked to the material's electronic properties.

In a recent development, "What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal," claims Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. "This demonstrates how the discovery of fresh materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.".

Why This Discovery Matters for Quantum Technology.

One of the biggest challenges in studying p-wave magnetism has been finding materials that display the necessary magnetic properties while remaining practical for detailed experiments.

Earlier candidates have included insulating materials, as well as metals that develop the required magnetic order only at extremely low temperatures or have complicated symmetries that make their behavior difficult to interpret.

EuSi offers a particularly useful combination of characteristics.

It is a stoichiometric metal, meaning its constituent elements occur in a fixed chemical ratio. Researchers can also grow high-quality single crystals of the material, and its spiral magnetic arrangement has the symmetry associated with p-wave magnetism.

Together, these features make EuSi a promising experimental platform for exploring how exotic magnetic states influence the behavior of electrons.

Theoretical studies suggest that metallic p-wave magnets could display several remarkable properties. For example, they may allow electrons with particular spin orientations to carry electrical currents without requiring an external magnetic field.

They could also produce strong changes in spin polarization when an electric current is applied, potentially offering new ways to manipulate electronic behavior.

These possibilities are especially relevant to spintronics, a field of technology that seeks to use electron spin, rather than electrical charge alone, to process and store information.

Another intriguing possibility involves unconventional superconductivity, in which electrical current flows without resistance through superconducting states that differ from those found in conventional superconductors.

Sources indicate that importantly, these predicted effects have not yet been demonstrated in EuSi. The discovery does not establish that the material can already perform these functions, but it gives researchers a promising system in which to test the predictions.

More broadly, the findings highlight how much of a material's behavior can remain hidden beneath an apparently simple chemical composition.

A solid's properties depend on more than the elements it contains or how its atoms are positioned. The arrangement of magnetic moments, the symmetries they create, and the quantum behavior of electrons can also produce entirely unexpected effects.

By revealing compelling evidence of p-wave magnetism in EuSi, researchers have gained a fresh opportunity to investigate these relationships and explore how unusual magnetic structures might eventually be used to control the electronic properties of future materials.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

Recent findings suggest that hoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Industry observers note that aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's upgrade.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that "I'm always happy to keep playing him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Avengers: Doomsday is fast approaching, and everyone seems pretty convinced Bucky Barnes isn't making it out alive.

Sebastian Stan has a role in The Batman 2, which set off alarm bells for Marvel fans that the Winter Soldier might not be returning for more in the MCU – and now an upgrade from Stan himself only seems to seal the deal.

Sources indicate that "I'm always happy to keep playing him. I don't know if the decision's up to me, ultimately," Stan noted on the Next Best Picture podcast.

When prompted by the interviewer that he must have some sway, Stan mentioned: "Well, I don't know, to be honest with you. I'm ready to take the character in all kinds of different ways, but I can't make that decision, it's the powers that be. And I think they have a lot going on, they have a lot on their plate. Do I feel we've explored that character, there's nowhere else to go, I think we did our best? I do think we've done our best so far.

"I don't think that that character totally got to fully live out his arc in the way that he has in the comics for instance, or that I've wanted," he continued. "I've been a big fan of the whole Black Widow of it all. But that's not the only way, you could take him in all kinds of ways. I've spoken about this Sicario-esque paranoid thriller where he just recognizes this person on the street and thinks it's a torturer from Hydra, like back in the day, and he becomes obsessed and starts following the person and realizes the person has a family. And then he's like, 'Am I crazy or is this the guy…?' and confronts the person, the guy denies it.

"Kevin just sort of went, "Sounds good, uh, we'll see,'" he added with a laugh. "So, I'm always ready, but we're at that point now where I can feel it, he needs to either evolve somewhere, or maybe it's time. It's one of those.".

Now, while it sounds like Stan still has tons of ideas when it comes to Bucky Barnes, it also certainly sounds like he's made peace with leaving the character behind. We'll find out when Avengers: Doomsday finally arrives on December 18.

In the meantime, check out our guide to all the upcoming Marvel movies and TV shows for everything else the MCU has in store.

Horu is a sci-fi 4X RTS inspired by Star Wars: Empire at War in which spaceships are spellcasters who can summon black holes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clicking a random link this morning, I was dazzled by the glare of a thousand laser batteries firing simultaneously.
  • But then I realised that I wasn't looking at a live newsfeed, but merely the Steam page for Horu, a real-time 4X strategy game in which you can "command hundreds of thousands of units across land and space", in the summary of developer David "GlassBeaver" Nadaski.
  • In development for years, and running on a custom C++ engine, Horu is inspired by 2006 hybrid RTS Star Wars: Empire at War - good, not great, in the words of turncoat jankonaut Graham, and the subject of many mods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clicking a random link this morning, I was dazzled by the glare of a thousand laser batteries firing simultaneously. My ears trembled beneath the trundle of a million caterpillar tracks. Balls of ice, bolts of lightning, shipments of rare alloys, and cascades of drop pods went screaming down my nerves and detonated in my frontal cortex, painting starlanes across the inside of my skull. "Oh god, they've finally found us!" I yelled, hiding beneath my desk. "I for one welcome our newly introduced galactic overlords!".

But then I realised that I wasn't looking at a live newsfeed, but merely the Steam page for Horu, a real-time 4X strategy game in which you can "command hundreds of thousands of units across land and space", in the summary of developer David "GlassBeaver" Nadaski. There's also a magic system, this being "the spice that makes your enemy's defeat bitter", which is a very genteel way to characterise glaciating a tank formation or conjuring a miniature blackhole.

In development for years, and running on a custom C++ engine, Horu is inspired by 2006 hybrid RTS Star Wars: Empire at War - good, not great, in the words of turncoat jankonaut Graham, and the subject of many mods. Horu's way of bettering Empire at War is seemingly to add a shedload more of everything. You can engage in a fleet battle that looks like two migrating ant hives colliding, even as a frankly unnecessary quantity of cyborgs pour over the forgeworld beneath and get their shit kicked in by some tornado-summoning sorcerers.

It has been revealed that offensives appear to work like this: any drop ships that push through the fleet battle add meat to the ground invasion, with the option of deploying wormholes to sneak your troops behind the defending armada. On the ground, you're basically out to capture control points. You're allegedly spared from "continuous babysitting" by semi-autonomous squadron commanders and an orders system that lets you queue up objectives, before units engage in battle.

Sources indicate that you can still give individual orders to units, but that seems like a recipe for acute wrist injury. There's also a boarding action mechanic whereby your hijackers move through vessels room by room. Again, I struggle to understand how you'll have time and dexterity to oversee such skulduggery when there are a bajillion particle cannons going off all at once.

According to recent reports, outside of combat, there are planets to develop, shipyards to build, spy networks to groom, research trees to water, and stock markets to manipulate. It all looks like business as usual for an imperial 4X. Honestly, I can imagine the maximalist warfaring being a hot mess, and then there's the fact that the dev is running a Kickstarter "to fund the remaining assets needed for a playable build: more spaceships, more units, more animations, more sounds, more music, and everything in between." I've been burned by Kickstarter overpromising before. Still, I can only admire the vindictive intellect that would have me play a little game of FTL inside what looks like one of the larger PvP scraps from Eve Online.

You can read more on Steam. Release date there is at the moment none. For an equally populous strategy experience that's closer in style to Supreme Commander, check out Sanctuary: Shattered Space.

Cannabis owners develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug.
  • The findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney.
  • Recent findings suggest that psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug. Even more concerning, the difference becomes substantially larger with age, reaching more than six years among people who develop psychosis in their 30s or later.

The findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney. They suggest that the potential psychiatric consequences of cannabis use may extend well beyond adolescence and could become more pronounced with prolonged exposure.

Recent findings suggest that psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations, false beliefs known as delusions, and disturbances in thinking or behavior. It can occur in schizophrenia and several other mental health disorders. Although psychosis most commonly begins during the late teenage years or early adulthood, it can develop at other stages of life. According to Psychosis Australia, up to 3% of adults will experience a diagnosed disorder involving psychosis during their lifetime.

Cannabis Linked to Earlier Psychosis Across Adulthood.

Sources indicate that to investigate the relationship between cannabis use and the timing of psychosis, researchers at UNSW Medicine analyzed 149 studies involving more than 71,000 participants. Most of the research had been conducted since 2011 in Europe, North America, and Australia, with the majority of studies focusing on people diagnosed with schizophrenia.

The researchers discovered that the difference in the age at which psychosis first appeared varied considerably across age groups.

According to recent reports, in studies where the average age of psychosis onset was between 20 and 24, cannabis people experienced their first episode approximately 1.6 years earlier than non-users. That difference widened to 4.43 years in studies involving people whose psychosis emerged in their mid-to-late 20s (25-29).

Recent findings suggest that the largest difference appeared in studies where psychosis developed at age 30 or later. In this group, cannabis users experienced the condition an average of 6.3 years earlier than non-users.

These results suggest that the association between cannabis and earlier psychosis may become stronger as people grow older, potentially reflecting the effects of longer periods of cannabis exposure.

Why Cannabis Risks May Increase With Age.

Chief investigator Matthew Large, a psychiatrist and Conjoint Professor at UNSW's School of Clinical Medicine, mentioned the findings raise key questions about the long-term psychiatric effects of cannabis.

Industry observers note that "We've tended to focus on the dangers of using cannabis in adolescence, when the brain is still developing, but the risk doesn't disappear once you're in your 20s," Prof. Large remarked. "What we're seeing suggests a cumulative effect, where harm builds up over time, a bit like alcohol or nicotine.".

Interestingly, the analysis did not identify a statistically significant difference in the timing of psychosis between teenage cannabis consumers and teenagers who did not use cannabis.

However, the researchers cautioned that this finding does not necessarily mean younger cannabis users face no risk. Psychosis rarely develops before the middle teenage years, leaving relatively little opportunity for its onset to shift to an even younger age.

"There may be a biological floor, in that there is only so much earlier that onset can be shifted. In younger groups, strong development, genetic or other psychosis risk factors may dominate, making any cannabis-related age shift harder to detect," Prof. Large said.

The researchers also stressed an key limitation. Because the analysis examined existing observational studies, it cannot establish that cannabis directly causes psychosis or makes the condition begin sooner. Demonstrating such a relationship experimentally would require research that deliberately exposed people to potential psychiatric harm, which would be unethical.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, Prof. Large believes the overall pattern provides meaningful evidence supporting a possible causal connection.

"But the consistency of the evidence, particularly the strong effect in older adults who likely have been using cannabis for longer, does support the theory that cannabis plays a causal role in the timing of psychosis onset, and possibly the onset of some cases among people who would not have otherwise developed psychosis.".

Upcoming Findings Challenge Assumptions About Cannabis After Age 25.

The latest research builds on two earlier investigations into cannabis use and the development of psychosis.

According to recent reports, in a smaller 2011 meta-analysis led by Prof. Large, researchers found that psychosis began approximately 2.7 years earlier among cannabis consumers. A separate 2015 analysis reported that psychosis typically developed 6.3 years after cannabis use began.

However, neither earlier investigation had enough information to determine how the relationship differed across age groups.

By incorporating a much larger body of research, the new analysis allowed scientists to examine how the association changes across different stages of adulthood.

Lead author Carly Stevens, from UNSW's School of Biomedical Sciences, stated the findings undermine the idea that avoiding cannabis during adolescence is sufficient to eliminate its potential psychiatric dangers.

It has been revealed that "What we've found challenges the assumption that you'll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s; that's just not the case," Ms. Stevens noted.

"There's been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is important, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone.".

Why Even a Few Years of Delayed Psychosis Matter.

Although a difference of two or three years might initially seem relatively small, the researchers emphasized that the timing of psychosis can have profound consequences for a person's future.

The late teenage years and early adulthood are often periods when people complete their education, begin careers, establish relationships, and develop greater independence. Experiencing a serious psychiatric disorder earlier in life can interrupt these key milestones.

It has been revealed that "People may miss out on study, job opportunities, travel, and relationships in those years, and treatment can come with physical side effects that can make life harder as well," Ms. Stevens said.

Sources indicate that prof. Large emphasized the potential benefits of reducing or discontinuing cannabis use and the importance of delaying the onset of psychosis wherever possible.

"It's a major illness, which robs you of your shared reality with family, friends and all those around you," he stated. "If we can delay psychosis by even a few years, people will be more likely to reach crucial milestones in education and training, and develop strong support networks, which can protect against psychosocial decline.".

The potential benefits could also extend to healthcare systems. According to Prof. Large, psychotic disorders account for as much as 3% of health-related spending in developed countries. Preventing or delaying the onset of these conditions could therefore have substantial social and economic benefits.

Scientists Call for Stronger Cannabis Health Warnings.

Despite the inability to establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship, the researchers believe their findings provide sufficient justification for stronger warnings about the possible psychiatric consequences of cannabis use.

Industry observers note that "We can't run direct experiments, so we have to go with the best evidence available," Prof. Large said. "In my view, the threshold for health warnings about cannabis and psychosis has definitely been met.".

Recent findings suggest that one concern is the growing popularity of medical cannabis. Prof. Large stated its increasing use as a therapeutic product may encourage some people to assume that it carries little risk.

He has also observed an increasing number of patients receiving treatment for psychosis who had previously been prescribed cannabis for medical conditions where evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited.

"It's got this therapeutic halo around it, which blinds people to the risk.".

Another emerging concern involves cannabis edibles, which can contain elevated concentrations of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main compound responsible for the drug's mind altering effects. The availability of products containing higher THC concentrations raises additional questions about possible psychiatric risks.

At the same time, Prof. Large acknowledged that cannabis legalization could create opportunities to reduce harm, even though it would also make cannabis easier to obtain.

Legal regulation could allow governments to establish limits on product potency, improve consumer education, introduce taxation, and require buyers to receive clear information about potential health consequences.

"You could tax it, regulate it, and require people to show they understand the risks before buying," Prof. Large said.

More Research Needed on Long-Term Cannabis Exposure.

The researchers say further studies are necessary to understand the biological processes that might explain why the association between cannabis use and earlier psychosis becomes more pronounced with age.

In particular, they want to investigate whether repeated or prolonged cannabis exposure produces cumulative changes that influence when psychotic symptoms emerge.

They also recommend additional research focusing on older cannabis customers, an increasingly key population as medical cannabis becomes more common and products containing high concentrations of THC become more widely available.

It has been revealed that another priority is improving how cannabis exposure is measured. The researchers argue that future studies need clearer and more consistent methods for recording cannabis consumption so that findings can be compared more reliably.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the newly introduced analysis highlights an notable gap in public understanding of cannabis and mental health. While warnings have traditionally concentrated on teenage use, the findings suggest that potential psychiatric risks deserve attention throughout adulthood, particularly among people who continue using cannabis over many years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another fresh entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

It has been revealed that the Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

In a recent development, the gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet fresh characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

According to recent reports, the game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

It has been revealed that you can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game rolls out. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.
